::: {.question-card}
### Question $1$

A veterinary clinic classifies each arriving patient by species and visit type. For this exercise, the only possible outcomes are

$$
S=\{CR,CE,DR,DE\}
$$

where $C$ means cat, $D$ means dog, $R$ means routine visit and $E$ means emergency visit. Let $A$ be the event that the patient is a cat and let $B$ be the event that the visit is an emergency.

1. Write events $A$ and $B$ as sets of outcomes.
2. Write $A\cap B$ as a set and describe it in words.
3. Write $A\cup B$ as a set and describe it in words.
4. Write $A^c$ as a set and describe it in words.
5. Are $A$ and $B$ disjoint? Explain.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The events are

  $$
  A=\{CR,CE\}
  $$

  $$
  B=\{CE,DE\}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The intersection is

  $$
  A\cap B=\{CE\}
  $$

  It represents an emergency visit involving a cat.</li>
  <li>The union is

  $$
  A\cup B=\{CR,CE,DE\}
  $$

  It represents a visit involving a cat, an emergency visit or both.</li>
  <li>The complement is

  $$
  A^c=\{DR,DE\}
  $$

  It represents a visit involving a dog.</li>
  <li>The events are not disjoint because $CE$ belongs to both events. Therefore, $A\cap B$ is not empty.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $2$

A wildlife rehabilitation centre records whether each admitted animal is eventually released ($R$) or is not released ($R^c$). Suppose

$$
P(R)=0.82
$$

1. Calculate $P(R^c)$.
2. Calculate $P(R\cap R^c)$.
3. Calculate $P(R\cup R^c)$.
4. Are $R$ and $R^c$ disjoint? Are they exhaustive?
5. Are $R$ and $R^c$ independent? Justify your answer mathematically.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Using the complement rule,

  $$
  P(R^c)=1-0.82=0.18
  $$
  </li>
  <li>An animal cannot be both released and not released, so

  $$
  P(R\cap R^c)=0
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The two events cover every possible outcome, so

  $$
  P(R\cup R^c)=1
  $$
  </li>
  <li>They are disjoint because they cannot occur together. They are exhaustive because one of them must occur.</li>
  <li>They are not independent. If they were independent, their intersection would satisfy

  $$
  P(R\cap R^c)=P(R)P(R^c)=(0.82)(0.18)=0.1476
  $$

  The actual intersection probability is $0$, not $0.1476$. Two disjoint events with positive probabilities cannot be independent.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $3$

A physics laboratory uses two independent safety sensors. During a normal operating period, Sensor $A$ has probability $0.02$ of producing a false alarm and Sensor $B$ has probability $0.03$ of producing a false alarm.

1. What is the probability that both sensors produce false alarms during the same period?
2. What is the probability that neither sensor produces a false alarm?
3. What is the probability that at least one sensor produces a false alarm?
4. What is the probability that exactly one sensor produces a false alarm?
5. Which step requires the independence assumption?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Independence gives

  $$
  P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=(0.02)(0.03)=0.0006
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The probabilities of no false alarm are $0.98$ and $0.97$. Therefore,

  $$
  P(A^c\cap B^c)=(0.98)(0.97)=0.9506
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Using the complement rule,

  $$
  P(A\cup B)=1-P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-0.9506=0.0494
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Exactly one false alarm can occur along either of two disjoint paths:

  $$
  P(A\cap B^c)+P(A^c\cap B)
  $$

  $$
  =(0.02)(0.97)+(0.98)(0.03)=0.0488
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Independence is required whenever the marginal probabilities are multiplied to obtain a joint probability, including the calculations for both alarms, neither alarm and each exactly-one path.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $4$

A veterinary laboratory tests $150$ samples known not to contain a particular pathogen. The false-positive probability for one sample is $0.006$. Assume the test outcomes are independent from sample to sample.

1. What is the probability that one pathogen-free sample tests negative?
2. What is the probability that all $150$ samples test negative?
3. What is the probability that at least one false positive occurs?
4. Interpret the answer to Part $3$ in context.
5. Explain why multiplying $150$ by $0.006$ does not give the probability of at least one false positive.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The probability of a correct negative is

  $$
  1-0.006=0.994
  $$
  </li>
  <li>By independence,

  $$
  P(\text{all negative})=(0.994)^{150}\approx0.4055
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The complement of at least one false positive is no false positives:

  $$
  P(\text{at least one false positive})=1-(0.994)^{150}\approx0.5945
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Under this model, there is approximately a $59.45\%$ probability that at least one of the $150$ pathogen-free samples produces a false-positive result.</li>
  <li>The product $150(0.006)=0.9$ is the expected number of false positives, not the probability of at least one. A count can have an expected value of $0.9$ even though the probability of one or more occurrences is different.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $5$

At $400$ wildlife-monitoring sites, researchers detected red foxes at $168$ sites, coyotes at $124$ sites and both species at $52$ sites. Let $F$ be the event that a randomly selected site had a fox detection and let $C$ be the event that it had a coyote detection.

1. Calculate $P(F)$, $P(C)$ and $P(F\cap C)$.
2. Calculate the probability that at least one of the two species was detected.
3. How many sites had neither species detected?
4. How many sites had only foxes detected?
5. How many sites had only coyotes detected?
6. Explain why adding $168$ and $124$ without subtracting $52$ would be incorrect.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The probabilities are

  $$
  P(F)=\frac{168}{400}=0.42
  $$

  $$
  P(C)=\frac{124}{400}=0.31
  $$

  $$
  P(F\cap C)=\frac{52}{400}=0.13
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Using the General Addition Rule,

  $$
  P(F\cup C)=0.42+0.31-0.13=0.60
  $$

  Therefore, $240$ sites had at least one species detected.</li>
  <li>The number with neither species is

  $$
  400-240=160
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The number with foxes only is

  $$
  168-52=116
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The number with coyotes only is

  $$
  124-52=72
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The $52$ sites containing both species are included in both marginal counts. Direct addition would count those sites twice, so the overlap must be subtracted once.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $6$

A hypothetical veterinary study of Dalmatians reports

$$
P(I)=0.24
$$

$$
P(B)=0.15
$$

$$
P(I\cap B)=0.06
$$

where $I$ means hearing impairment and $B$ means blue eyes.

1. Calculate $P(I\cap B^c)$, the probability of hearing impairment without blue eyes.
2. Calculate $P(I^c\cap B)$, the probability of blue eyes without hearing impairment.
3. Calculate the probability of neither trait.
4. Verify that the four disjoint regions sum to $1$.
5. Verify the partition identity $P(I)=P(I\cap B)+P(I\cap B^c)$.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The hearing-impairment event is partitioned by blue-eye status:

  $$
  P(I\cap B^c)=P(I)-P(I\cap B)=0.24-0.06=0.18
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Similarly,

  $$
  P(I^c\cap B)=P(B)-P(I\cap B)=0.15-0.06=0.09
  $$
  </li>
  <li>First calculate the union:

  $$
  P(I\cup B)=0.24+0.15-0.06=0.33
  $$

  Therefore,

  $$
  P(I^c\cap B^c)=1-0.33=0.67
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The four disjoint regions are impairment only, both traits, blue eyes only and neither:

  $$
  0.18+0.06+0.09+0.67=1
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The identity is verified because

  $$
  P(I\cap B)+P(I\cap B^c)=0.06+0.18=0.24=P(I)
  $$
  </li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $7$

A veterinary hospital records gastrointestinal symptoms and laboratory-confirmed parasitic infection for $300$ dogs.

| Infection status | Diarrhea | No diarrhea | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Parasitic infection | $54$ | $36$ | $90$ |
| No parasitic infection | $42$ | $168$ | $210$ |
| **Total** | **$96$** | **$204$** | **$300$** |

Let $I$ mean parasitic infection and let $D$ mean diarrhea.

1. Calculate $P(I)$ and $P(D)$.
2. Calculate $P(I\cap D)$.
3. Calculate $P(I\mid D)$ and interpret it.
4. Calculate $P(D\mid I)$ and interpret it.
5. Why are the answers to Parts $3$ and $4$ different even though they use the same intersection count?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The marginal probabilities are

  $$
  P(I)=\frac{90}{300}=0.30
  $$

  $$
  P(D)=\frac{96}{300}=0.32
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The joint probability is

  $$
  P(I\cap D)=\frac{54}{300}=0.18
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Conditioning on diarrhea restricts the denominator to the $96$ dogs with diarrhea:

  $$
  P(I\mid D)=\frac{54}{96}=0.5625
  $$

  Among dogs with diarrhea, $56.25\%$ had a laboratory-confirmed parasitic infection.</li>
  <li>Conditioning on infection restricts the denominator to the $90$ infected dogs:

  $$
  P(D\mid I)=\frac{54}{90}=0.60
  $$

  Among dogs with a parasitic infection, $60\%$ had diarrhea.</li>
  <li>Both calculations use the $54$ dogs in the intersection, but their denominators differ. Part $3$ uses all dogs with diarrhea, whereas Part $4$ uses all infected dogs.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $8$

Ecologists examine $100$ farms. Native bees are detected at $50$ farms, pesticide use is classified as low at $40$ farms and both conditions occur at $28$ farms. Let $N$ mean native bees were detected and let $L$ mean pesticide use was low.

1. Calculate $P(N)$, $P(L)$ and $P(N\cap L)$.
2. If $N$ and $L$ were independent, what would $P(N\cap L)$ equal?
3. Are $N$ and $L$ independent? Explain.
4. Calculate $P(N\mid L)$ and compare it with $P(N)$.
5. Under independence, how many of the $100$ farms would be expected to have both characteristics? How does this compare with the observed count?
6. Does the association establish that low pesticide use causes native-bee detection? Explain briefly.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The probabilities are

  $$
  P(N)=0.50
  $$

  $$
  P(L)=0.40
  $$

  $$
  P(N\cap L)=0.28
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Under independence,

  $$
  P(N)P(L)=(0.50)(0.40)=0.20
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The events are not independent because

  $$
  P(N\cap L)=0.28\neq0.20=P(N)P(L)
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The conditional probability is

  $$
  P(N\mid L)=\frac{0.28}{0.40}=0.70
  $$

  Native bees were detected at $70\%$ of low-pesticide farms, compared with $50\%$ of all farms. Conditioning on $L$ changes the probability of $N$.</li>
  <li>Independence would predict

  $$
  100(0.20)=20
  $$

  farms with both characteristics. The observed count is $28$, which is $8$ higher.</li>
  <li>No. The data show an association, but other variables such as crop type, habitat quality, floral resources and farm size may affect both pesticide use and bee detection.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $9$

In a wetland survey, $35\%$ of sites are temporary wetlands. Among temporary wetlands, a threatened frog species is detected at $62\%$ of sites. Let $T$ mean temporary wetland and let $F$ mean frog detection.

1. Calculate $P(T\cap F)$.
2. Interpret $P(T\cap F)$ in context.
3. Calculate $P(T\cap F^c)$.
4. Verify that $P(T\cap F)+P(T\cap F^c)=P(T)$.
5. In a survey of $1200$ sites with the same proportions, approximately how many sites would be both temporary and have a frog detection?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Use the General Multiplication Rule:

  $$
  P(T\cap F)=P(T)P(F\mid T)=(0.35)(0.62)=0.217
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Approximately $21.7\%$ of all surveyed sites are temporary wetlands where the frog species is detected.</li>
  <li>Within temporary wetlands,

  $$
  P(F^c\mid T)=1-0.62=0.38
  $$

  Therefore,

  $$
  P(T\cap F^c)=(0.35)(0.38)=0.133
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The two disjoint pieces sum to the temporary-wetland probability:

  $$
  0.217+0.133=0.350=P(T)
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The expected count is

  $$
  1200(0.217)=260.4
  $$

  Approximately $260$ sites would be expected to have both characteristics.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $10$

A wildlife rehabilitation organization summarizes release outcomes for $240$ animals.

| Animal group | Released | Not released | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Birds | $84$ | $36$ | $120$ |
| Mammals | $54$ | $36$ | $90$ |
| Reptiles | $12$ | $18$ | $30$ |
| **Total** | **$150$** | **$90$** | **$240$** |

1. Calculate the overall release probability.
2. Calculate the conditional release probability within each animal group.
3. Among released animals, calculate the conditional distribution of animal group.
4. Which animal group has the highest release rate? Which group contributes the largest number of released animals?
5. Are animal group and release outcome independent? Demonstrate using one conditional probability.
6. Explain why the table alone does not establish that animal group causes the difference in release outcomes.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The overall release probability is

  $$
  P(R)=\frac{150}{240}=0.625
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The within-group release probabilities are

  $$
  P(R\mid\text{bird})=\frac{84}{120}=0.70
  $$

  $$
  P(R\mid\text{mammal})=\frac{54}{90}=0.60
  $$

  $$
  P(R\mid\text{reptile})=\frac{12}{30}=0.40
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Among the $150$ released animals,

  $$
  P(\text{bird}\mid R)=\frac{84}{150}=0.56
  $$

  $$
  P(\text{mammal}\mid R)=\frac{54}{150}=0.36
  $$

  $$
  P(\text{reptile}\mid R)=\frac{12}{150}=0.08
  $$

  These values sum to $1$.</li>
  <li>Birds have the highest release rate at $70\%$. Birds also contribute the largest number of released animals, with $84$ releases.</li>
  <li>The variables are not independent. For example,

  $$
  P(R\mid\text{bird})=0.70\neq0.625=P(R)
  $$

  Knowing that an animal is a bird changes the observed release probability.</li>
  <li>Injury severity, species, age, admission reason and treatment options may differ across animal groups. The table describes an association and does not isolate a causal effect of animal group.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $11$

A veterinary laboratory receives a tray containing $20$ blood samples, of which $5$ are visibly hemolyzed. A technician selects $3$ samples without replacement for immediate review.

1. What is the probability that all $3$ selected samples are not hemolyzed?
2. What is the probability that at least one selected sample is hemolyzed?
3. What is the probability that the first sample is not hemolyzed and the second sample is hemolyzed?
4. If selection were instead performed with replacement, what would be the probability of at least one hemolyzed sample in $3$ selections?
5. Explain why the draws are dependent when sampling without replacement.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>There are $15$ non-hemolyzed samples. Without replacement,

  $$
  P(\text{all three not hemolyzed})
  =\frac{15}{20}\frac{14}{19}\frac{13}{18}
  \approx0.3991
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Using the complement rule,

  $$
  P(\text{at least one hemolyzed})
  =1-0.3991
  \approx0.6009
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The required sequence has probability

  $$
  P(\text{first good and second hemolyzed})
  =\frac{15}{20}\frac{5}{19}
  \approx0.1974
  $$
  </li>
  <li>With replacement, the probability of a non-hemolyzed result remains $15/20=0.75$ on every draw:

  $$
  P(\text{at least one hemolyzed})
  =1-(0.75)^3
  =0.5781
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Without replacement, each selection changes both the number and composition of the remaining samples. Therefore, the probability for the next draw depends on what was selected earlier.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $12$

A laboratory quality-control device produces two binary indicators on each calibration run. The four ordered pairs

$$
(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,0),\ (1,1)
$$

are equally likely. Define the following events:

- $A$: the first indicator equals $1$
- $B$: the second indicator equals $1$
- $C$: the two indicators agree

1. List the outcomes in $A$, $B$ and $C$.
2. Find $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(C)$.
3. Show that each pair of events is independent.
4. Calculate $P(A\cap B\cap C)$.
5. Compare the answer from Part $4$ with $P(A)P(B)P(C)$.
6. What does this example demonstrate about pairwise and mutual independence?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The events are

  $$
  A=\{(1,0),(1,1)\}
  $$

  $$
  B=\{(0,1),(1,1)\}
  $$

  $$
  C=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Each event contains $2$ of the $4$ equally likely outcomes, so

  $$
  P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{2}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Each pairwise intersection contains one outcome:

  $$
  P(A\cap B)=P(A\cap C)=P(B\cap C)=\frac{1}{4}
  $$

  For every pair,

  $$
  \frac{1}{4}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)
  $$

  Therefore, $A$, $B$ and $C$ are pairwise independent.</li>
  <li>All three events occur only for the outcome $(1,1)$, so

  $$
  P(A\cap B\cap C)=\frac{1}{4}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The product of the three marginal probabilities is

  $$
  P(A)P(B)P(C)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{1}{8}
  $$

  This differs from $P(A\cap B\cap C)=1/4$.</li>
  <li>The example shows that pairwise independence does not guarantee mutual independence. The three-event product rule requires the stronger mutual-independence condition.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $13$

An animal rehabilitation centre classifies an admitted animal as having a severe injury ($S$) with probability $0.25$ and a non-severe injury ($S^c$) with probability $0.75$. The probability of recovery within $48$ hours is $0.60$ for a severe injury and $0.90$ for a non-severe injury. Let $R$ mean recovery within $48$ hours.

1. Draw a tree diagram showing injury severity followed by recovery status. Label every branch.
2. Calculate the four joint probabilities at the ends of the tree.
3. Calculate $P(R)$.
4. Calculate $P(S\mid R)$.
5. Explain why $P(S\mid R)$ is not equal to $P(R\mid S)$.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The first branches are $S$ with probability $0.25$ and $S^c$ with probability $0.75$. From $S$, the recovery branches have probabilities $0.60$ and $0.40$. From $S^c$, they have probabilities $0.90$ and $0.10$.</li>
  <li>Multiplying along each path gives

  $$
  P(S\cap R)=(0.25)(0.60)=0.150
  $$

  $$
  P(S\cap R^c)=(0.25)(0.40)=0.100
  $$

  $$
  P(S^c\cap R)=(0.75)(0.90)=0.675
  $$

  $$
  P(S^c\cap R^c)=(0.75)(0.10)=0.075
  $$

  The four path probabilities sum to $1$.</li>
  <li>The two recovery paths are disjoint:

  $$
  P(R)=0.150+0.675=0.825
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Among animals that recovered within $48$ hours,

  $$
  P(S\mid R)=\frac{P(S\cap R)}{P(R)}
  =\frac{0.150}{0.825}
  \approx0.1818
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The probability $P(R\mid S)=0.60$ uses all severely injured animals as its denominator. The probability $P(S\mid R)\approx0.1818$ uses all animals that recovered within $48$ hours as its denominator. The conditioning groups are different.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $14$

A physics laboratory routes calibration measurements through three instruments. Instrument $A$ processes $40\%$ of measurements and has error probability $0.01$. Instrument $B$ processes $35\%$ and has error probability $0.025$. Instrument $C$ processes $25\%$ and has error probability $0.04$.

Let $E$ mean that a randomly selected measurement contains an error.

1. Calculate $P(A\cap E)$, $P(B\cap E)$ and $P(C\cap E)$.
2. Use the Law of Total Probability to calculate $P(E)$.
3. Given that an error occurred, calculate the probability that the measurement came from Instrument $B$.
4. Given that an error occurred, which instrument is the most likely source?
5. Why is Instrument $C$ not automatically responsible for most errors simply because it has the highest within-instrument error rate?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The joint path probabilities are

  $$
  P(A\cap E)=(0.40)(0.01)=0.0040
  $$

  $$
  P(B\cap E)=(0.35)(0.025)=0.00875
  $$

  $$
  P(C\cap E)=(0.25)(0.04)=0.0100
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The three instrument groups form a partition, so

  $$
  P(E)=0.0040+0.00875+0.0100=0.02275
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Using the error group as the denominator,

  $$
  P(B\mid E)=\frac{0.00875}{0.02275}\approx0.3846
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Instrument $C$ has the largest error-path probability, $0.0100$. Therefore,

  $$
  P(C\mid E)=\frac{0.0100}{0.02275}\approx0.4396
  $$

  Instrument $C$ is the most likely source of an observed error.</li>
  <li>The number of errors contributed by an instrument depends on both its within-instrument error rate and the proportion of all measurements it processes. A high conditional error rate may be offset by a small processing share.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $15$

An automobile insurer divides its policyholders into three age groups. The figures below are hypothetical.

| Age group | Proportion of policyholders | Annual claim probability |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Under $25$ | $0.18$ | $0.22$ |
| Ages $25$--$64$ | $0.57$ | $0.10$ |
| Age $65$ or older | $0.25$ | $0.14$ |

Let $C$ mean that a policyholder files a claim during the year.

1. Calculate the joint probability of belonging to each age group and filing a claim.
2. Calculate $P(C)$.
3. Given that a claim was filed, calculate the probability that it came from each age group.
4. Which age group has the highest individual claim probability?
5. Which age group contributes the largest share of all claims? Explain why the answers to Parts $4$ and $5$ differ.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The three claim-path probabilities are

  $$
  P(\text{under }25\cap C)=(0.18)(0.22)=0.0396
  $$

  $$
  P(25\text{--}64\cap C)=(0.57)(0.10)=0.0570
  $$

  $$
  P(65+\cap C)=(0.25)(0.14)=0.0350
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The overall claim probability is

  $$
  P(C)=0.0396+0.0570+0.0350=0.1316
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The reverse conditional probabilities are

  $$
  P(\text{under }25\mid C)=\frac{0.0396}{0.1316}\approx0.3009
  $$

  $$
  P(25\text{--}64\mid C)=\frac{0.0570}{0.1316}\approx0.4331
  $$

  $$
  P(65+\mid C)=\frac{0.0350}{0.1316}\approx0.2660
  $$

  These probabilities sum to $1$.</li>
  <li>The under-$25$ group has the highest within-group claim probability, $0.22$.</li>
  <li>The ages-$25$--$64$ group contributes the largest share of claims, approximately $43.31\%$, because it is much larger than either of the other groups. Claim contribution depends on both group size and within-group claim probability.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $16$

A veterinary clinic screens dogs for heartworm. In the population being screened, the prevalence is $4\%$. The test has sensitivity $95\%$ and specificity $97\%$.

Let $H$ mean heartworm infection and let $+$ and $-$ represent positive and negative test results.

1. Write the sensitivity, specificity and false-positive probability using conditional probability notation.
2. For $10000$ screened dogs, construct the expected counts of true positives, false negatives, false positives and true negatives.
3. Calculate $P(+)$.
4. Calculate the positive predictive value $P(H\mid +)$.
5. Calculate the negative predictive value $P(H^c\mid -)$.
6. Interpret both predictive values in context.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The test characteristics are

  $$
  P(+\mid H)=0.95
  $$

  $$
  P(-\mid H^c)=0.97
  $$

  Therefore,

  $$
  P(+\mid H^c)=1-0.97=0.03
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Among $10000$ dogs, $400$ are expected to have heartworm and $9600$ are expected not to have it.

  $$
  \text{True positives}=400(0.95)=380
  $$

  $$
  \text{False negatives}=400(0.05)=20
  $$

  $$
  \text{False positives}=9600(0.03)=288
  $$

  $$
  \text{True negatives}=9600(0.97)=9312
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The overall positive probability is

  $$
  P(+)=P(H)P(+\mid H)+P(H^c)P(+\mid H^c)
  $$

  $$
  =(0.04)(0.95)+(0.96)(0.03)=0.0668
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The positive predictive value is

  $$
  P(H\mid +)=\frac{0.04(0.95)}{0.0668}
  =\frac{0.038}{0.0668}
  \approx0.5689
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The probability of a negative result is

  $$
  P(-)=(0.04)(0.05)+(0.96)(0.97)=0.9332
  $$

  Therefore,

  $$
  P(H^c\mid -)=\frac{(0.96)(0.97)}{0.9332}
  =\frac{0.9312}{0.9332}
  \approx0.9979
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Among dogs with a positive result, approximately $56.89\%$ are expected to have heartworm under this model. Among dogs with a negative result, approximately $99.79\%$ are expected not to have heartworm.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $17$

The same rapid test is used in two animal shelters. The test has sensitivity $0.90$ and specificity $0.95$ in both shelters. Disease prevalence is $0.02$ in Shelter $A$ and $0.15$ in Shelter $B$.

1. Calculate the false-positive probability.
2. Calculate the positive predictive value in Shelter $A$.
3. Calculate the positive predictive value in Shelter $B$.
4. Why do the predictive values differ even though the test has the same sensitivity and specificity?
5. If $10000$ animals were screened at each shelter, approximately how many true positives and false positives would occur at each shelter?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The false-positive probability is

  $$
  P(+\mid D^c)=1-0.95=0.05
  $$
  </li>
  <li>For Shelter $A$,

  $$
  P(D\mid +)
  =\frac{(0.02)(0.90)}{(0.02)(0.90)+(0.98)(0.05)}
  =\frac{0.018}{0.067}
  \approx0.2687
  $$
  </li>
  <li>For Shelter $B$,

  $$
  P(D\mid +)
  =\frac{(0.15)(0.90)}{(0.15)(0.90)+(0.85)(0.05)}
  =\frac{0.135}{0.1775}
  \approx0.7606
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as test accuracy. In Shelter $A$, the disease-free group is much larger and produces many false positives relative to the number of true positives. The higher prevalence in Shelter $B$ increases the proportion of positive results that are true positives.</li>
  <li>At Shelter $A$,

  $$
  \text{True positives}=10000(0.02)(0.90)=180
  $$

  $$
  \text{False positives}=10000(0.98)(0.05)=490
  $$

  At Shelter $B$,

  $$
  \text{True positives}=10000(0.15)(0.90)=1350
  $$

  $$
  \text{False positives}=10000(0.85)(0.05)=425
  $$
  </li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $18$

An environmental agency receives water samples from three source types. Half come from Treatment Plant $A$, $30\%$ come from Treatment Plant $B$ and $20\%$ come from private wells. The probabilities of dangerous contamination are $0.01$, $0.04$ and $0.12$, respectively.

Let $D$ mean dangerous contamination.

1. Calculate the joint probability of each source type and dangerous contamination.
2. Use the Law of Total Probability to calculate $P(D)$.
3. Given that a sample is dangerously contaminated, calculate the probability that it came from each source type.
4. Which source type is most likely for a contaminated sample?
5. Among $10000$ samples, how many dangerously contaminated samples would be expected from each source type?
6. Explain why the most common source of all samples is not necessarily the most common source among contaminated samples.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The contamination paths are

  $$
  P(A\cap D)=(0.50)(0.01)=0.005
  $$

  $$
  P(B\cap D)=(0.30)(0.04)=0.012
  $$

  $$
  P(W\cap D)=(0.20)(0.12)=0.024
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The overall probability is

  $$
  P(D)=0.005+0.012+0.024=0.041
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The reverse conditional probabilities are

  $$
  P(A\mid D)=\frac{0.005}{0.041}\approx0.1220
  $$

  $$
  P(B\mid D)=\frac{0.012}{0.041}\approx0.2927
  $$

  $$
  P(W\mid D)=\frac{0.024}{0.041}\approx0.5854
  $$
  </li>
  <li>A contaminated sample is most likely to have come from a private well, with conditional probability approximately $0.5854$.</li>
  <li>Among $10000$ samples, the expected contaminated counts are

  $$
  10000(0.005)=50
  $$

  from Plant $A$,

  $$
  10000(0.012)=120
  $$

  from Plant $B$ and

  $$
  10000(0.024)=240
  $$

  from private wells.</li>
  <li>Source frequency and contamination rate both matter. Plant $A$ provides the largest number of samples, but its contamination probability is much lower than the private-well probability.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $19$

A medical study uses two screening tests for the same condition. Disease prevalence is $0.08$. Test $1$ has sensitivity $0.90$ and specificity $0.95$. Test $2$ has sensitivity $0.85$ and specificity $0.98$.

Assume that the two test results are independent **conditional on the person's true disease status**. A person receives positive results on both tests.

1. Calculate $P(T_1^+\cap T_2^+\mid D)$.
2. Calculate $P(T_1^+\cap T_2^+\mid D^c)$.
3. Calculate the probability of disease and two positive results.
4. Calculate the probability of no disease and two positive results.
5. Use Bayes's Theorem to calculate $P(D\mid T_1^+\cap T_2^+)$.
6. Explain precisely which independence assumption was used. Why would multiplying the two unconditional positive-test probabilities be incorrect?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Conditional independence within the disease group gives

  $$
  P(T_1^+\cap T_2^+\mid D)=(0.90)(0.85)=0.765
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The false-positive probabilities are $0.05$ and $0.02$. Conditional independence within the disease-free group gives

  $$
  P(T_1^+\cap T_2^+\mid D^c)=(0.05)(0.02)=0.001
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The disease-and-two-positive path has probability

  $$
  P(D\cap T_1^+\cap T_2^+)=(0.08)(0.765)=0.0612
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The disease-free-and-two-positive path has probability

  $$
  P(D^c\cap T_1^+\cap T_2^+)=(0.92)(0.001)=0.00092
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The posterior probability is

  $$
  P(D\mid T_1^+\cap T_2^+)
  =\frac{0.0612}{0.0612+0.00092}
  \approx0.9852
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The assumption states that the two test results are independent after disease status is fixed. It permits multiplication within the $D$ branch and within the $D^c$ branch. The test results are not necessarily independent in the overall population because both are related to the same underlying disease status. Multiplying unconditional positive probabilities would ignore that shared structure.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $20$

Wildlife veterinarians screen animals for an infectious disease in three habitats. The following values are hypothetical.

| Habitat | Proportion of screened animals | Disease prevalence within habitat |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Forest | $0.50$ | $0.06$ |
| Wetland | $0.30$ | $0.15$ |
| Grassland | $0.20$ | $0.03$ |

The diagnostic test has sensitivity $0.92$ and specificity $0.96$ in every habitat. Let $D$ mean disease and let $+$ mean a positive test result.

1. Use the Law of Total Probability to calculate the overall disease prevalence $P(D)$.
2. Calculate the overall probability of a positive result, $P(+)$.
3. Calculate $P(D\mid +)$.
4. Calculate $P(\text{wetland}\cap D\cap +)$.
5. Calculate the total probability of a positive result arising from each habitat.
6. Given a positive result, calculate the probability that the animal came from a wetland.
7. Among wetland animals with a positive result, calculate the probability of disease.
8. Are habitat and disease status independent? Justify your answer using probabilities.
9. Explain why neither a positive result nor wetland origin alone should be interpreted as proof that an individual animal has the disease.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The overall disease prevalence is

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  P(D)
  &=(0.50)(0.06)+(0.30)(0.15)+(0.20)(0.03)\\
  &=0.030+0.045+0.006\\
  &=0.081
  \end{aligned}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The false-positive probability is $1-0.96=0.04$. Therefore,

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  P(+)
  &=P(D)P(+\mid D)+P(D^c)P(+\mid D^c)\\
  &=(0.081)(0.92)+(0.919)(0.04)\\
  &=0.11128
  \end{aligned}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The posterior probability of disease is

  $$
  P(D\mid +)=\frac{(0.081)(0.92)}{0.11128}\approx0.6697
  $$
  </li>
  <li>The wetland, disease and positive-test path has probability

  $$
  P(W\cap D\cap +)=(0.30)(0.15)(0.92)=0.0414
  $$
  </li>
  <li>For forest animals,

  $$
  P(F\cap +)=0.50\big[(0.06)(0.92)+(0.94)(0.04)\big]=0.0464
  $$

  For wetland animals,

  $$
  P(W\cap +)=0.30\big[(0.15)(0.92)+(0.85)(0.04)\big]=0.0516
  $$

  For grassland animals,

  $$
  P(G\cap +)=0.20\big[(0.03)(0.92)+(0.97)(0.04)\big]=0.01328
  $$

  As a check,

  $$
  0.0464+0.0516+0.01328=0.11128=P(+)
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Among all positive results,

  $$
  P(W\mid +)=\frac{0.0516}{0.11128}\approx0.4637
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Within the wetland-positive group,

  $$
  P(D\mid W\cap +)=\frac{0.0414}{0.0516}\approx0.8023
  $$
  </li>
  <li>Habitat and disease status are not independent because

  $$
  P(D\mid W)=0.15\neq0.081=P(D)
  $$

  Knowing the habitat changes the disease probability in this model.</li>
  <li>A positive result can be false, and most wetland animals are still disease-free before test information is considered. The probabilities describe uncertainty within groups; diagnosis of an individual requires the test result, the relevant population information and appropriate clinical or confirmatory assessment.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::
